overview.body:
**Māra** (*mara*) — Death, Temptation, Illusion · The Tempter, Lord of Death — is Buddhism's personification of everything that keeps beings bound: death, desire, and distraction, the Evil One who assailed the future Buddha under the Bodhi tree and has never stopped working since.[^1]

The name comes from the root √*mṛ*, ‘to die’: *māra*, ‘death, the one who causes death, the killer’. The Pāli texts know him also as **Namuci**, ‘he who does not let go’, and as **Pāpimā**, ‘the Evil One’ — three names for one office.[^2] His great scene is the night of the awakening, when he rode against the seated sage with his armies and his daughters and lost; but his subtler work is the daily one — the whispered suggestion, the timely fear, the offer of an easier road — and the tradition insists he is at once a real devaputta of the highest sense-sphere heaven and a name for the mind's own resistance to waking.

PuniCodex restores the name as **Māra** and serves its temple at [māra.com](https://xn--mra-1oa.com). The restoration keeps the long ā of the Sanskrit; the plain ASCII *mara* is a modern convenience of the early domain-name system, not an attested ancient spelling.[^2]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (New York: Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’.
Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. māra, √mṛ.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in Sanskrit and Pāli as **मार** (IAST *māra*): from the root √*mṛ*, ‘to die’, the noun *māra* means ‘death, killing, the killer’ — personified, the god of death and the tempter.[^1] His bynames complete the dossier: **Namuci**, ‘the one who does not let go’ — the old asura name the Pāli texts give him, death as grip rather than blow; **Pāpimā** (Pāli; Sanskrit *Pāpīyas*), ‘the Evil One’, the tradition's most common address; and in Pāli also **Kaṇha**, ‘the Dark One’, pairing him against the Buddha as darkness against light.[^2]

The Buddhist analysis later multiplied the name into four Māras: the Māra of the defilements (kleśa), the Māra of the aggregates (skandha), the Māra who is death (mṛtyu), and the devaputta Māra, the deity of the Paranimmitavasavattin heaven who commands the sense-world's delights. The multiplication is the doctrine: most of what ‘Māra’ does, the texts concede, the mind does to itself.[^3]

The ASCII form *mara* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Māra** recovers the long ā directly in the address bar. Because the restoration preserves vowel length the ASCII form loses, the name is classified Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **m** → **M** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **ā** — Long vowel ā
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The project holds the domain **māra.com** (xn--mra-1oa.com) as the canonical home of this name.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. māra, √mṛ.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Grammar and Dictionary, vol. 2 (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Māra, Namuci.

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈmaː.rə/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Mā-** — Bilabial [m] with long open [aː]; the root syllable of √mṛ, ‘to die’, stressed and held long
- **-ra** — Trilled or tapped [r] with short [ə]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: ‘MAA-ruh’ — the first vowel twice the length of the second.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit / Pāli** — मार / Māra, ‘death, the killer’; bynames Namuci, Pāpimā, Kaṇha
- **Sinhala** — Māra; **Thai** — Māra, whence *Māra* in the idiom ‘defeat Māra’ for any great overcoming
- **Tibetan** — bDud (Dü), the standard translation: ‘the Demon’

Māra is Tier 1 because the long ā is the name's very root: *māra* from *mṛ*, death itself, lengthened in the dying.

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. māra.

domains.body:
**Māra** is the lord of everything that binds: death first, but also desire, fear, and the ten thousand distractions by which a being talks itself out of waking.[^1]

### Death

His oldest office: mṛtyu-māra, the mortality that ends every project — the king of the sense-sphere because everything in it dies.

### Temptation

Kāma-māra: desire as strategy — the daughters Taṇhā (Craving), Aratī (Discontent), and Ragā (Passion) sent to do what armies could not.[^2]

### The Armies of the Mind

His ten armies in the Padhāna Sutta are psychological states: sense-pleasure, discontent, hunger and thirst, craving, sloth and torpor, fear, doubt, hypocrisy and obstinacy, self-seeking glory, and self-exalting contempt for others.[^2]

### The Household of Illusion

As devaputta of the Paranimmitavasavattin heaven he ‘controls what others create’ — the deity of a world where everything delightful is someone else's work, and nothing is free.

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’.
Sutta Nipāta 3.2 (Padhāna Sutta); Saṃyutta Nikāya 4 (Mārasaṃyutta).

symbols.body:
The iconography of Māra is the negative image of the Buddha's calm:[^1]

- **The elephant Girimekhala** — His war-mount at the Bodhi tree, the beast of the world's bulk thrown against one seated man
- **The demon army** — The grotesque host of Gandhāran reliefs and Thai murals: weapons that turn to flowers in mid-air over the Buddha's head
- **The daughters** — Taṇhā, Aratī, Ragā: Craving, Discontent, Passion, his three envoys of charm after force fails
- **The bow and flower-arrows** — Later art arms him as a dark inversion of the love-god: arrows that are blossoms, killing by attraction[^2]
- **The dark body** — Kaṇha, ‘the Dark One’: the iconographic shadow against the Buddha's gold

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’ and ‘Buddhist Art’.
Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (London: Allen & Unwin, 1962).

mythology.body:
Māra's mythology is the counter-narrative of the Buddha's whole career: wherever the Dharma advances, he is on the scene within a verse.[^1]

### The Assault under the Tree (Padhāna Sutta; Lalitavistara 21)

As the future [[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]] sat immovable beneath the Bodhi tree, Māra came in person. The Padhāna Sutta (Sn 3.2) has him name his armies — desire first, then discontent, hunger and thirst, craving, sloth and torpor, fear, doubt, hypocrisy and obstinacy, vainglory, and self-exalting contempt — and the Buddha answer that he would rather die in battle than live defeated. The Sanskrit Lalitavistara expands the night into epic: Girimekhala the elephant, the grotesque host, the weapons falling as flowers, the daughters sent after the rout — and the earth itself called to witness, quaking its testimony until the army breaks.[^2]

### The Daughters (SN 4.25)

Force having failed, Māra sent Taṇhā, Aratī, and Ragā — Craving, Discontent, Passion. The Buddha saw them as they were, and they withdrew as a crow withdraws from a stone it has pecked.[^3]

### The Persistent Tempter (Mārasaṃyutta; Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta)

The canon refuses to retire him. For forty-five years Māra returns: to the Buddha, suggesting that the Dharma is too deep to teach; to the nuns, taunting that women cannot awaken (Sister Somā's reply is one of the canon's great retorts); to the monks, as a snake in the grass, a voice in the ear, a sudden doubt. He is, in Ling's phrase, the mythology of evil domesticated into a working psychology.[^4]

### The Last Invitation (DN 16)

His final recorded success is the gentlest: at the Mahāparinibbāna he comes not with armies but with a courteous request — the Tathāgata has done his work; let him pass away now. The Buddha agrees, setting the date of the parinirvāṇa. The Tempter's last temptation is the one even the Buddha grants: everything compounded decays — and Māra, who is death, is owed his due.[^5]

sources.citation: Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’.
Sutta Nipāta 3.2 (Padhāna Sutta); Lalitavistara Sūtra, ch. 21.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.25 (Māradhītu Sutta), trans. Bhikkhu Bodhi (2000).
Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (Allen & Unwin, 1962).
Dīgha Nikāya 16 (Mahāparinibbāna Sutta), trans. Walshe (1995).

syncretism.body:
Māra is the closest figure Buddhism has to the Devil, and the comparison has been drawn since the first Western studies — but the tradition itself resists the equation: Māra creates no beings and damns no one, is subject to kamma like every other being, and in some Mahāyāna texts is himself converted and destined for Buddhahood. T. O. Ling's classic study maps the difference precisely: not a principle of evil opposed to God, but the personification of the forces within saṃsāra that resist awakening — a tempter inside the system, not a rebel against it.[^1]

The tantric tradition absorbed him into the protector cults (the subjugation of Māra is a standard maṇḍala rite), Tibetan tradition translates his name as bDud, ‘the demon’, and the comparative literature pairs his fourfold analysis — kleśa, skandha, mṛtyu, devaputta — with every psychology that distinguishes the enemy without from the enemy within. Kindred figures in the PuniCodex index include [[shakyamuni|Śākyamuni]] (the one he could not move) and [[thanatos|Thánatos]] (Greek death, his nearest structural cousin).

sources.citation: Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (Allen & Unwin, 1962).

cultural-legacy.body:
Māra's deepest legacy is therapeutic: the Buddhist analysis of temptation — the ten armies as states of mind — is a working psychology of distraction that modern meditation teaching uses daily, and ‘Māra’ has become the standard shorthand, in Dharma halls worldwide, for whatever shows up to pull the mind off the cushion.[^1] The Dhammapada's victory verses — ‘seeking the builder of this house I wandered through countless births... now you are seen, O builder; you shall not build again’ — remain the most quoted lines in the Pāli canon, the winner's speech over the Tempter.

His image built the iconography of the Buddha's greatest moment: the bhūmisparśa earth-touching gesture — the right hand down, calling the earth to witness against Māra — is the single most reproduced pose of the Buddha in Southeast Asia, the Tempter's defeat fixed as the teacher's emblem.[^2]

sources.citation: Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (Allen & Unwin, 1962).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’, ‘Buddhist Art’.

archaeology.body:
Māra's monuments are the assault scenes of Buddhist art. The Gandhāran schist reliefs (1st–3rd c. CE) established the composition: the serene seated Buddha at the centre, the grotesque host collapsing around him, weapons arrested mid-flight — the visual charter of every later Māravijaya (‘Victory over Māra’) scene.[^1]

The type then became Southeast Asia's signature: the great Māravijaya images of Bagan, Sukhothai, and the Thai and Burmese temple traditions, where the earth-touching Buddha — often with the earth-goddess Vasundharā wringing the flood of merit from her hair to drown the demon host — anchors the whole iconographic program. The armies of the murals, half nightmare and half carnival, are among the masterpieces of narrative painting in Asia.[^2]

sources.citation: Foucher, Alfred, L'art gréco-bouddhique du Gandhāra (Paris: Ernest Leroux, 1905–22).
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Buddhist Art’.

meditation.body:
Māra is the most psychologically honest figure in Buddhist mythology. The canon never lets him be merely a monster: his armies are moods, his daughters are cravings, his weapons are the ones the mind uses on itself. The night under the tree is everyone's night before any real change — the sudden appetite, the timely fear, the reasonable voice suggesting tomorrow.

What defeats him is not force but recognition. The Buddha does not fight the armies; he names them, touches the earth, and stays seated. The tradition's whole counsel on temptation is in that gesture: you do not have to win the argument with the voice — you have to know whose voice it is. Namuci, they called him: the one who does not let go. The answer to a grip is not a blow. It is not needing to pull free.

sources.citation: Sutta Nipāta 3.2 (Padhāna Sutta); Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (1962).

pali-canon.body:
Māra is everywhere in the Pāli Canon — the Tempter is one of its best-documented characters. The **Padhāna Sutta** (Sn 3.2) preserves the austere early account of the assault: Māra as Namuci addressing the striving Buddha with the eight-plus armies, each a state of mind, and the Buddha's answer that death in the struggle is better than life in retreat.[^1] The **Mārasaṃyutta** (SN 4) collects twenty-five short encounters across the whole teaching career — Māra as farmer, as herdsman, as meteor, as voice — including the daughters' embassy (4.25); the **Bhikkhunīsaṃyutta** (SN 5) records his ten taunts to the nuns and their triumphant dismissals.

The **Mahāparinibbāna Sutta** (DN 16) gives him the last word of the biography: his courteous request that the Buddha pass away now, and the Buddha's consent — death, even for the deathless teaching, arriving on schedule.[^2]

sources.citation: Sutta Nipāta 3.2; Bodhi, Bhikkhu, trans., The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (Wisdom, 2000): SN 4, SN 5.
Walshe, Maurice, trans., The Long Discourses of the Buddha (Wisdom, 1995): DN 16.

mahayana-sutras.body:
The Sanskrit tradition enlarged the assault into epic. The **Lalitavistara** (ch. 21) stages the night at Bodhgayā at full scale: the summons to the demon host, Girimekhala the elephant, the weapons turning to flowers, the earth shaking her witness — the version the art of Asia paints.[^1]

The Mahāyāna sūtras then interiorize him. The Perfection of Wisdom literature warns the bodhisattva against ‘Māra's deeds’ — subtle discouragements, spiritual pride, the temptation to abandon beings for private peace — and the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa teaches that the bodhisattva works precisely in Māra's fields, ‘among the hosts of Māra’ as among flowers. Some Mahāyāna texts go further and prophesy the devaputta Māra's own eventual awakening: the Tempter himself is not outside the Dharma's reach.[^2]

sources.citation: Lalitavistara Sūtra, ch. 21.
Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (Macmillan Reference, 2004), s.v. ‘Māra’; Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra.

commentarial-tradition.body:
The Pāli commentarial tradition built the canon's scattered encounters into the full biography: the **Nidānakathā**, Buddhaghosa's introduction to the Jātaka commentary, gives the Theravāda's complete narrative of the assault — the earth called to witness the perfections, the army's rout, the tree-deities' jubilation — and the commentaries on SN 4 gloss each apparition with the working psychology of meditation.[^1]

The systematic analysis belongs to the Abhidharma and śāstra traditions: the fourfold Māra — the defilements (kleśa), the aggregates (skandha), death (mṛtyu), and the devaputta deity — turns the myth into a diagnostic scheme in which three of the four Māras are internal, a framework the Mahāprajñāpāramitāśāstra and the Tibetan graduated-path literature made standard. T. O. Ling's modern study remains the standard interpretation: Buddhism's mythology of evil as the personified friction of a mind against its own liberation.[^2]

sources.citation: Nidānakathā of the Jātaka commentary; the commentaries on SN 4.
Ling, Trevor O., Buddhism and the Mythology of Evil (Allen & Unwin, 1962); Buswell, Robert E., ed., Encyclopedia of Buddhism (2004), s.v. ‘Māra’.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Devanagari as **मार** — Brahmic abugida, attested Sanskrit and Pāli (via the Brāhmī-derived scripts), in the Buddhist manuscript traditions of India; the script is written left-to-right.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Māra* (IAST), giving the normalized reading /ˈmaː.rə/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Sanskrit Māra is written मार in Devanagari: मा (mā) + र (ra), two open syllables; the vowel sign ा marks the long ā.
- The word derives from √mṛ, ‘to die’: māra, ‘death, the killer’ — personified, the Buddhist Tempter.
- IAST encodes vowel length with the macron (ā).
- The Unicode restoration Māra is registrable in .com; the Devanagari form is not supported in the .com IDN table.[^2]

sources.citation: Monier-Williams, Monier, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary (Clarendon Press, 1899), s.v. māra, √mṛ.
Edgerton, Franklin, Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit Dictionary (Yale University Press, 1953), s.v. Māra.
